In ''zoöl.'', an extensive, irregular, or otherwise notable migration into a place or country; an irruption, incursion, or invasion: as, a ''visitation'' of lemmings, of the Bohemian waxwing southward, or of the sand-grouse from Asia into France or England.—'''8.''' In ''her.'', an investigation by a high heraldic officer, usually one of the kings-at-arms, into the pedigrees, intermarriages, etc., of a family or the families of a district, with a view of ascertaining whether the arms borne by any person or persons living in that district are incorrect or unwarrantably assumed. {{smaller|The king-at-arms was accompanied on such occasions by secretaries, draftsmen, etc. The latest visitation on record in England seems to have been between the years 1686 and 1700; but before that time they had ceased to be regularly held.—'''Nuns of the Visitation, Order of the Visitation.''' Provision is made in the English Prayer-book for special confession and absolution of the sick person, while the American Prayer-book merely provides that the minister shall examine whether he repent him truly of his sins.}}

'''visiting''' (viz′i-ting), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''visit'', ''v.''] That visits; often, of persons, authorized to visit and inspect: as, a ''visiting'' committee.

'''visiting-ant''' (viz′i-ting-ȧnt), ''n.'' The driver-ant.

'''visiting-book''' (viz′i-ting-bu̇k), ''n.'' A book containing a list of names of persons who are to be called upon or who have called.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|visionary|6771|visiting-book}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|<poem>The ''visionary'' hour
When musing midnight reigns.</poem>{{right|''Thomson'', Summer, l. 556.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' Imaginative, romantic.—'''2.''' Unreal, fancied, ideal, illusory, utopian, chimerical.

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''visionaries'' (-riz). '''1.''' One who sees visions; one who lives in the imagination.
{{smaller block|<poem>To the ''Visionary'' seem
Her day-dreams truth, and truth a dream.</poem>{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, i. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|Aristophanes, so much of a scoffer and so little of a ''visionary''.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Lucian and Timotheus.}}}}
'''2.''' One who forms impracticable schemes; one who is given to idle and fanciful projects.
{{smaller block|Some celebrated writers of our country, who, with all their good sense and genius, were ''visionaries'' on the subject of education. {{right|''V. Knox'', Grammar Schools.}}}}
='''Syn.''' Dreamer, enthusiast.

'''visioned''' (vizh′ọnd), ''a.''   [< ''vision'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Having the power of seeing visions; hence, inspired. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh! not the ''visioned'' poet in his dreams . . .
So bright, so fair, so wild a shape
Hath yet beheld.</poem>{{right|''Shelley'', Queen Mab, i.}}}}
'''2.''' Seen in a vision; formed by the fancy, or in a dream, trance, or the like; produced by a vision; spectral.
{{smaller block|<poem>My ''vision’d'' sight might yet prove true.</poem>{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iv. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The dream
Of dark magician in his ''visioned'' cave.</poem>{{right|''Shelley'', Alastor.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She moves through fancy’s ''visioned'' space.</poem>{{right|''Lowell'', Fact or Fancy?}}}}

'''visionist''' (vizh′ọn-ist), ''n.''   [< ''vision'' + ''-ist''.]   One who sees, or believes that he sees, visions; a believer in visions; a visionary person.
{{smaller block|We are so far from attaining any certain and real knowledge of incorporeal beings (of an acquaintance with which these ''visionists'' so much boast) that we are not able to know anything of corporeal substances as abstract from their accidents. {{right|''Bp. Parker'', Platonick Philos., p. 66.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''visionist'' has deeper thoughts and more concealed feelings than these rhapsodical phantoms.
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Amen. of Lit., I. 215.}}}}

'''visionless''' (vizh′o̤n-les), ''a.''   [< ''vision'' + ''-less''.]   Destitute of vision; sightless; blind.

'''visit''' (viz′it), ''v.''   [< ME. ''visiten'', < OF. (and F.) ''visiter'' = Sp. Pg. ''visitar'' = It. ''visitare'', < L. ''visitare'', see, go to see, visit, punish, freq. of ''visere'', look at attentively, behold, < ''videre'', pp. ''visus'', see: see ''vision''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To go or come to see (a person or thing) in the way of friendship, business, curiosity, ceremony, or duty; call upon; proceed to in order to view or look on.
{{smaller block|And by the waye we ''vysyted'' some holy places.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|At lyons I ''visityd'' the Reliques at the yle wher Sent Anne lyes and longious.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I was sick, and ye ''visited'' me. {{right|Mat. xxv. 36.}}}}
{{smaller block|We will ''visit'' you at supper-time.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 2. 215.}}}}
{{smaller block|His wife was the rich china-woman that the courtiers ''visited'' so often. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To come or go to, in general; appear in or at; enter.
{{smaller block|Amana is more familiar, and entreth the Citie—yea, by help of art, in Conduits ''visiteth'' their priuate houses.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 237.}}}}
{{smaller block|For me, in showers, in sweeping showers, the spring
''Visits'' the valley. {{right|''Emerson'', Musketaquid.}}}}

'''3.''' To go or come to see for the purpose of inspection, supervision, examination, correction of abuses, or the like; examine; inspect.

{{smaller block|I may excite your princely cogitations to ''visit'' the excellent treasure of your own mind.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|Achmet would not suffer the bales intended for the king of Abyssinia to be opened or ''visited'', but left them in the hands of the ambassador.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 506.}}}}

'''4.''' To afflict; overtake or come upon: said especially of diseases or calamities.

<poem>Ere he by sickness had been ''visited''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 1. 26.}}}}
<poem>''Face.'' The house, sir, has been ''visited''.
''Love.'' What, with the plague?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, v. 1.}}}}
<poem>’Tis a house here
Where people of all sorts, that have been ''visited''
With lunacies and follies, wait their cures.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Pilgrim, iii. 6.}}}}

'''5.''' In Scriptural phraseology: (''a'') To send a judgment from heaven upon, whether for the purpose of chastising or afflicting, or of comforting or consoling; judge.

{{smaller block|Oh ''visit'' me with thy salvation. {{right|Ps. cvi. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Therefore hast thou ''visited'' and destroyed them.
{{right|Isa. xxvi. 14.}}}}

(''b'') To inflict punishment for (guilt) or upon (a person).

{{smaller block|I am persuaded that God has ''visited'' you with this punishment for my ungodliness.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Works (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 354.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Visiting'' the iniquity of the fathers upon the children.
{{right|Ex. xxxiv. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now will he remember their iniquity, and ''visit'' their sins.
{{right|Hos. viii. 13.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To practise going to see others; keep up friendly intercourse by going to the houses of friends; make calls; stay with (another) as a guest.
{{smaller block|Whilst she was under her mother she was forced to be genteel, to live in ceremony, . . . and always ''visiting'' on Sundays.
{{right|''Law'', Serious Call, viii.}}}}

'''visit''' (viz′it), ''n.''   [< F. ''visite'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''visita''; from the verb.]   '''1.''' The act of visiting or going to see a person, place, or thing; a temporary residence in a locality or with some one as a guest; a call on a person or at a place.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’m come to take my last farewell,
And pay my last ''visit'' to thee.</poem>
{{right|''Young Hunting'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 295).}}}}
{{smaller block|I’d sooner be visited by the Plague; for that only wou’d keep a man from ''Visits'', and his Doors shut.
{{right|''Wycherley'', Plain Dealer, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Visits''
Like those of angels, short and far between.</poem>
{{right|''Blair'', The Grave, ii. 589.}}}}

'''2.''' A formal or official call; a visitation.
{{smaller block|Periodical ''visits'' were made by vassals to their suzerains, and by these to their higher suzerains — the kings.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 379.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Domiciliary visit.''' See ''domiciliary''.—'''Right of visit.''' Same as ''right of visitation''. See ''visitation'', 5.—'''Visit to the Blessed Sacrament,''' in ''Rom. Cath. usage'', a daily visit to a church in order to engage in silent prayer before the sacrament: a practice common in religious houses.}}

'''visitable''' (viz′i-ta-bl), ''a.''   [< ''visit'' + ''-able''.]   Liable or subject to be visited or inspected; admitting of visitation or inspection.
{{smaller block|The next morning we set out again, in order to see the Sanctuaries and other ''visitable'' places upon Mount Olivet.
{{right|''Maundrell'', Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 104.}}}}
{{smaller block|All hospitals built since the reformation are ''visitable'' by the king or lord chancellor. {{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon.}}}}

'''visitant''' (viz′i-tant), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< L. ''visitan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''visitare'', see: see ''visit''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Acting the part of a visitor; paying visits; visiting.
{{smaller block|<poem>He knew the rocks which Angels haunt
Upon the mountains ''visitant''.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Song at Feast of Brougham Castle.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One who visits; one who goes or comes to see another; one who is a guest in the house of a friend; a visitor.
{{smaller block|<poem>You have private ''visitants'', my noble lady,
That in sweet numbers court your goodly virtues.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|He has a rich wrought waistcoat to entertain his ''visitants'' in. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The intellectual character of her extreme beauty, . . . and her unbounded benevolence, gave more the idea of an angelic ''visitant'' than of a being belonging to this nether world. {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M. (ed. 1830), Int.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His heart,
Where Fear sat thus, a cherished ''visitant''.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, i.}}}} '''2.''' In ''ornith.'', a migratory bird which comes to and stays in a place or region during a part of the year: opposed to ''resident'': as, the snowy owl is a winter ''visitant'' from the north in the United States. Rare or irregular visitants are termed ''stragglers.'' See ''straggler'', 2.—'''3.''' [''cap.''] A member of a Roman Catholic order of nuns, founded at Annecy in Savoy by Francis de Sales and Mme. de Chantal in 1610. {{smaller|The order spread in various countries, and has been efficient in the education of young girls. The Visitants are also called ''Salesians'', ''Order of the Visitation'', ''Nuns of the Visitation'', etc.}}

'''visitation''' (viz-i-tā′shọn), ''n.''   [< ME. ''visitacioun'', < OF. (and F.) ''visitation'' = Sp. ''visitacion'' = Pg. ''visitação'' = It. ''visitazione'', < LL. ''visitatio''(''n''-), a sight, appearance, visitation, punishment, < L. ''visitare'', visit: see ''visit.'']   '''1.''' The act of visiting, or paying a visit; a visit.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therfore I made my ''visitaciouns''
To vigilies and to processiouns.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 555.}}}}
{{smaller block|The king of Sicilia means to pay Bohemia the ''visitation'' which he justly owes him. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 1. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|When a woman is deliuered of a child, the man lyeth in and keepeth his bed, with ''visitation'' of Gossips, the space of fortie dayes. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 429.}}}}
'''2.''' The object of a visit. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>O flowers, . . .
My early ''visitation'', and my last.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 275.}}}}

'''3.''' A formal or judicial visit paid periodicall by a superior, superintending officer, or othe competent authority, to a corporation, college church, or other house, for the purpose of examining into the manner in which the busines of the body is conducted, and its laws and reg ulations are observed and executed, or the like; specifically (''eccles.''), such examination by a bishop of the churches in his diocese, with the added purpose of administering confirmation. {{smaller|The right of visitation attaches to metropolitans in their provinces, to bishops in their dioceses, and to archdeacons in certain cases.}}
{{smaller block|The magistrates shall be more familiar and open each to other, and more frequent in ''visitations'', and shall, in tenderness and love, admonish one another.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 213.}}}}
'''4.''' A special dispensation from heaven, sometimes of divine favor, more usually of divine retribution; divine retributive affliction; hence, a similar incident of less importance, whether joyful or grievous.
{{smaller block|We see that the most comfortable ''visitations'' which God hath sent men from above have taken especially the times of prayer as their most natural opportunities.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|What will ye do in the day of ''visitation'', and in the desolation which shall come from far? {{right|Isa. x. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|These were bright ''visitations'' in a scholar’s and a clerk’s life. {{right|''Lamb'', Oxford in the Vacation.}}}}
'''5.''' In ''international law'', the act of a naval commander who visits or boards a vessel belonging to another state for the purpose of ascertaining her character and object. {{smaller|It does not include the claim or exercise of the right of search. The right of performing this act is called the ''right of visit'' or ''of visitation.''} '''6.''' [''cap.''] A church festival in honor of the visit of the Virgin Mary to her cousin Elizabeth (Luke i. 39), celebrated on July 2d in the Roman Catholic, Greek, and other churches.—'''7.''' In ''zoöl.'', an extensive, irregular, or otherwise notable migration into a place or country; an irruption, incursion, or invasion: as, a ''visitation'' of lemmings, of the Bohemian waxwing southward, or of the sand-grouse from Asia into France or England.—'''8.''' In ''her.'', an investigation by a high heraldic officer, usually one of the kings-at-arms, into the pedigrees, intermarriages, etc., of a family or the families of a district, with a view of ascertaining whether the arms borne by any person or persons living in that district are incorrect or unwarrantably assumed. {{smaller|The king-at-arms was accompanied on such occasions by secretaries, draftsmen, etc. The latest visitation on record in England seems to have been between the years 1686 and 1700; but before that time they had ceased to be regularly held.—'''Nuns of the Visitation, Order of the Visitation.''' See ''visitant'', 3.—'''Visitation of the sick''', an office of the Anglican Church, appointed to be used for the spiritual benefit of sick persons. Provision is made in the English Prayer-book for special confession and absolution of the sick person, while the American Prayer-book merely provides that the minister shall examine whether he repent him truly of his sins.}}

'''visitatorial''' (viz″i-tā-tō′ri-al), ''a.''   [< LL. ''visitator'', a visitor (< L. ''visitare'', see), + ''-i-al''.]   Belonging or pertaining to a judicial visitor or visitation: as, ''visitatorial'' power; hence, pertaining to any authorized inspector or examination: as, a health officer’s ''visitatorial'' work or authority. Also ''visitorial.''
{{smaller block|The enactment by which Elizabeth and her successors had been empowered to appoint commissioners with ''visitatorial'' authority over the Church was not only not revived, but was declared, with the utmost strength of language, to be completely abrogated.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}

'''visit-day''' (viz′it-dā), ''n.'' A day on which callers are received.
{{smaller block|<poem>On ''visit-days'' she bears
To mount her fifty flights of ample stairs.</poem>
{{right|''Parnell'', Elegy to an Old Beauty.}}}}

'''visite''' (vi-zēt′), ''n.''   [F., visit: see ''visit.'']   An outer garment worn by women in the first half of the nineteenth century, thin, made of silk or like material, and shaped to the person.

'''visiter''' (viz′i-tėr), ''n.''   [< ''visit'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''visitor.'']   Same as ''visitor''.
{{smaller block|His ''visiter'' observed the look, and proceeded.
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}

'''visiting''' (viz′i-ting), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''visit, v.'']   '''1.''' The act or practice of paying visits or making calls. Also used adjectively.
{{smaller block|The business of her life was to get her daughters married: its solace was ''visiting'' and news.
{{right|''Jane Austen'', Pride and Prejudice, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|Our ancestors are very good kind of folks; but they are the last people I should choose to have a ''visiting'' acquaintance with.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Prompting; influence.
{{smaller block|<poem>No compunctious ''visitings'' of nature
Shake my fell purpose. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 5. 46.</poem>}}

'''visiting''' (viz′i-ting), ''p. a.''   [Ppr. of ''visit'', ''v.'']   That visits; often, of persons, authorized to visit and inspect: as, a ''visiting'' committee.

'''visiting-ant''' (viz′i-ting-ȧnt), ''n.'' The driver-ant.

'''visiting-book''' (viz′i-ting-bu̇k), ''n.'' A book containing a list of names of persons who are to be called upon or who have called.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
